The phenomenon of ocean tides is primarily driven by the gravitational interaction between the Earth and the Moon, although the Sun also plays a secondary role. To understand how the Moon causes tides, one must look beyond the simple idea that the Moon "pulls" the water toward it. If gravity were the only factor, the entire Earth, including its oceans, would simply accelerate toward the Moon. Instead, tides arise due to **tidal forces**, which are the differences in gravitational pull across the Earth’s diameter.

The Moon’s gravity is stronger on the side of the Earth facing the Moon than it is on the center of the Earth. This stronger pull on the near side causes the ocean water to bulge outward, creating a high tide. Simultaneously, on the side of the Earth facing away from the Moon, the gravitational pull is weaker than at the Earth’s center. However, because the Earth and Moon orbit their common center of mass (the barycenter), the Earth is effectively being "left behind" by the water on the far side. This results in a second bulge of water on the opposite side of the Earth, creating another high tide.
